utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we go into closed session this morning, Mr. Visnjic, just to confirm the matter that arose yesterday. The Chamber will sit on the application by the United Kingdom for an extension of time and take no action on it. It's for you then to trigger any further action by drawing our attention to a failure to resolve this. We will also expect you to resolve to our attention if you are successful in resolving the matter, so we can clear it from our outstanding list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We will inform you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will now go into closed session so the witness can enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tanic. Your cross-examination will now continue. I anticipate a number of counsel will have questions to ask of you. Please remember how much we already know. Please try not to repeat yourself. You're entirely free, as you know, to justify your conduct and actions in response to questions by specifying your reason for doing things. But please, in doing so, endeavour to concentrate your answer on the point that arises rather than repeat what's been said before. Please also bear in mind that the solemn declaration which you took at the outset continues to apply to your evidence throughout that evidence. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can I ask that the usher place before Mr. Tanic the bundle of exhibits with ten tabs and the English and B/C/S version of his statement P2480.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the full statement or only the first --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's the full statement in both languages with numbered paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, yesterday we were talking about what you describe as the discreet negotiations with the Kosovar Albanians, and I believe you told the Court that these negotiations took place between 1995 and the end of 1997. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, P2480, at paragraph 5, you say that in addition to you and Dusan Mihajlovic, a man named Dojcilo Maslovaric, the Yugoslav envoy to the Vatican, and Professor Ratko Markovic, the deputy prime minister of Serbia, were also appointed to conduct discreet negotiations with the Kosovar Albanians. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dojcilo Maslovaric and Ratko Markovic, they participated in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You also told the Court that these discreet negotiations took place within the context of meetings organised by the Bertelsmann Foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And for the record, I refer to exhibits P704, P705, P707, P708, P709, and P718. These are newspaper articles and documents produced at the Bertelsmann meetings on Kosovo, including the programme of the meetings held between 1995 and 1998, as well as the names of speakers and participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tanic, would it surprise you to learn that the names of Dusan Mihajlovic, Dojcilo Maslarovic, and Mr. Markovic do not appear in any of these exhibits?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but what you said is untrue. I never said that they participated in any other negotiations, except from those carried out within the Bertelsmann Science Foundation. It was just one of the NGO groups which were engaged in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... carry on now. It seems to be on the screen, but it's just probably me that's not getting it for some reason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Bertelsmann Foundation was just one of the NGOs which acted on behalf of the German foreign ministry. I also mentioned the negotiations led by Mr. Paglia as well as some direct meetings, and what you saw is untrue. I never said that these particular negotiations were within the framework of the Bertelsmann Foundation, and I would ask the Bench to warn the Defence not to put words in my mouth, especially not those that I didn't say. I explained how it worked. The Bertelsmann Foundation was only one of the institutions involved, and Mr. Dojcilo Maslarovic and Ratko Markovic appeared in that phase of the negotiations which was led by Monsignor Paglia, where I participated as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. In your statement at paragraph number 5, you state on some occasions you, Mr. Maslarovic, and Mr. Markovic worked together in discreet negotiations, the three of you. Now, give me a location, a date, and the substance of the negotiations that the three of you participated in together. Give me an example.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I mentioned on several occasions that Maslarovic, Markovic, and I worked together; that's all I said. Now you seem to be adding up; for example, when Mr. Markovic and I worked together, and Dojcilo participated in it subsequently, it was at a meeting with the German and the British ambassador. I would have to consult my notes again on that. There was another international community representative. It was a working lunch, and we discussed the Kosovo issue. Negotiations on that occasion were directly involving the international community. I had some contact with Maslarovic and -- within in a different context as well, but I never said that all three of us sat at the same table in the same phase of negotiations. Defence is trying to say that I said something I didn't, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Give me one example where you and these two men sat down with the Albanians and had a meeting to discuss Kosovo. I want a date, a place, and the substance of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When did I ever tell you that all three of us were at the same table with the Albanian side? With all due respect for the Bench and Defence, I cannot answer untruthful questions, questions based on imagination, on something invented. If you want me to name the people there, there was the German and the British ambassador, on behalf of the international community, and Branko Brankovic, on behalf of the Serbian foreign ministry. I would have to consult my notes to tell you when and that's when we discussed Kosovo, with the international community involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, there are a number of misunderstandings in your mind reflected in that answer. The question was not about occasions when you sat down at the table with the Albanian side. The question was about when the three of you sat down together and discussed Kosovo. And you seem to have identified one occasion when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, the most recent question was an example where you and the two men sat down with the Albanians, page 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're quite right, Mr. Hannis. Sorry, I overlooked that. Now, Mr. O'Sullivan, the statement doesn't actually say that, does it? If I read your statement to you, Mr. Tanic, you'll understand why the questions are being asked the way they are nevertheless. "On some occasions, Maslarovic, Markovic, and I worked together; however, they also spoke with Kosovo Albanian representatives independently on other occasions." Now, it's easy to form the impression there that you were saying that all three of you had discussions with Albanians. I think I understand your position to be now that that did not happen, and the only meeting at which you were present with these other two involved the German and British ambassador. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was together with Markovic on several occasions, but Defence asked me to specify a single example. As for Dojcilo Maslarovic, there were two or three working meetings with him concerning negotiations conducted by Mr. Paglia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, the question is about when all three of you were together. Is there more than one occasion when all three of you were involved in negotiations together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Not the three of us together, and I never said that. I said we worked together --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and Mr. O'Sullivan is abusing the use of the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tanic, that is an unacceptable remark.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We worked together on the programme led by Vicenzo Paglia, on behalf of the Vatican. We never sat at the same table together, but we worked on it. You can ask Monsignor Paglia to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you testified in the Milosevic trial on the 14th, 15th, 16th, and 21st of May, 2002. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, we looked at paragraphs 4 and 5 of your statement, right at the end of your testimony yesterday, where you described your authorisation to conduct discreet negotiations. Let me remind you about one sentence in paragraph 4. "In summary, my political authorisation to conduct these negotiations came from three sources: Milosevic, the SDB, and my party, because it was officially part of the government."

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like to refer to Exhibit 1D30, Your Honour. In hard copy that's tab number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Behind tab number 3, Mr. Tanic, we have first an English language document and second the Serbian language document. This document was produced by the information service of New Democracy in Belgrade on the 14th of May, 2002. I want to look at this with you. First, the title of this document is -- and you'll see the document is stamped and signed in the original by a representative of New Democracy. The title of the document is: "Imagination Is Everything." First sentence: "Regarding the testimony of Mr. Ratomir Tanic in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic in The Hague, New Democracy would like to remind the public of a few facts." Then I go to the second paragraph, first sentence: "The second fact relates to Ratomir Tanic, a founder of the UJDI, Association for Yugoslav democratic initiative, a reformist and vice-president of the Civic Alliance of Serbia, who only became a New Democracy sympathiser in 1995 and joined its sector for international relations." Now, if we stop there and go back to Exhibit 1D31, the record sheet we looked at yesterday, you can see that this statement by New Democracy describes you as a sympathiser, the same way you were described in the information sheet which you signed; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is correct? That this document describes me or that I was a sympathiser?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a non-productive avenue, Mr. O'Sullivan. We can read these documents. We can see the relationship between the two. This is the sort of thing is not going to advance matters, bearing in mind how long it took to deal with this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm still in the second paragraph of this exhibit, 1D30, and I'll read from the last portion, the last sentence or phrases of that second paragraph. It says here: "There was no plans to resolve the Kosmat problem, nor was anyone authorised to make such plans on behalf of New Democracy with anyone, including the people mentioned by Mr. Ratomir Tanic. Ratko Markovic, Dojcilo Maslarovic, Jovica Stanisic, Momcilo Perisic, Mira Markovic, Slobodan Milosevic, or representatives on diplomatic missions in our country. No one in New Democracy was informed of Mr. Tanic's relations with domestic and foreign services, so his," and the word is illegible, "activity has no connection whatsoever with his involvement in New Democracy's international activities." I move to the second page, the penultimate paragraph, first sentence: "It's up to the Tribunal to assess the authenticity of Mr. Tanic's testimony, and New Democracy has nothing to do with this, as it does not wish to turn the trial into a circus, where witnesses will be at the level of newspaper articles and information published in the media." And finally the last sentence: "The stories told by Mr. Tanic have been told all over the media and thousands of citizens of this country could repeat them as hearsay." Now, Mr. Tanic, your party, New Democracy, denounces you as an imposter, don't they?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, perhaps it would be best for you to call here the representatives of New Democracy as your witnesses. I cannot offer any comment on this -- well, I could, but it would be ridiculous. Did you know how many people were killed in Serbia concerning the negotiations and peaceful solutions for Kosovo? Of course they have to denounce me, otherwise there goes their head. But please do call them here as witnesses. I'd be happy to. Call Mr. Mihajlovic to testify. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, this is an interesting document, because the part that you omitted to read - and I understand why you omitted it; it's not a criticism - makes the point that the witness was a participant in discussions between the Serbian and Albanian side. He maintained his contacts with the organisation -- organisers of these gatherings and continued attending them. Endeavours to resolve the problems in Kosovo and Metohija as peacefully and to reach a compromise between the Serbian and Albanian sides with the support of the international community are public policies of New Democracy and have been stated by all representatives of New Democracy, including Mr. Tanic. There were no plans to resolve the Kosmat problem, nor was anyone else authorised to make such plans on behalf of New Democracy with anyone. One has to ask the question: What is this all about? What is this press release all immediately about after the Milosevic evidence? Is it, as the witness said, New Democracy for political reasons trying to distance itself, and yet at the same time reap the benefits of one of their members being involved in peaceful negotiations? I don't know how much one can make of this sort of press release, quite frankly, or press reports, indeed. If we hear the witnesses, it might be a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Throughout your testimony, sir, you've invoked the name of Dusan Mihajlovic many times, in fact you just did a moment ago. Now, Mr. Mihajlovic gave an interview on live television in Belgrade on the evening of the 15th of May, 2002. And Exhibit 1D29 is the Milosevic transcript of the 21st of May, 2002, it's tab 4 of the hard copy. Now, the video-clip was played for you in court of this live broadcast that took place the night before, and here's what Mr. Mihajlovic had to say on television. "Well, you see the Hague Tribunal is a very serious institution that the world expects a lot of. It has invested a lot of time, money, and hope in it. And you see what is happening to us now, to find ourself in a rather ridiculous or sad situation that the Prosecution is loudly announcing a key witness, somebody who cannot be that, who has simply collected what he found in the newspapers and preparing his book on the Crisis Staff in Kosovo has actually made it available to the Tribunal. So this is mixing apples and pears, mixing political negotiations with the Albanian side organised by various foundations all over the world and other efforts that were made to avoid a conflict, to avoid the bombing, and so on. "But in any event, neither did Mr. Tanic take part in that, nor was he an active executor of any plans that he refers to. So this is rumours and hearsay that calls into question the Prosecution. This cannot be established in any way, because he did not participate in any way in the decision-making that he's testifying about, nor in the execution of those decisions. He was just an observer, like most -- like almost all of the citizens of Serbia. If that is an exaggeration, then anyone who took part in public and political life can be compared with him and this can be found in articles and programmes in the media." Now, here Mr. Mihajlovic denounces you as an imposter, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the Bench's permission, I'd like to comment on this statement, since I find it most interesting, item by item. First of all, in this statement Mr. Mihajlovic confirms that there were various talks, negotiations, and efforts to resolve the Kosovo Crisis by peaceful means. As for my participation in the effort, that is easy to prove, if one asks the institutions involved. And could you please all direct your attention to the following. It is often heard that what I testify about is something found in newspapers. It would have been true, had I testified back in 2004 or 2003 or 2005. Since in those years, I could have been able to read all that in the papers. However, my statement goes as far back as 1999 and the beginning of 2000. Any expert, independent expert, would tell you that at least 40 to 50 percent of the things I testified about in 2000, I couldn't have read anywhere, in no book or newspaper, because some things were highly secretive. Only after 2002 these things began seeing the light of day, and indeed in 2002 I could have read them. But I spoke to The Hague Tribunal about that in 1999 and 2000. First and foremost, this involves the peace plan to end the war. It appeared for the first time in Lilic's book in 2002, and I spoke about it with the OTP in 2000, when no one knew about it. Also, some elements which were used or attempted to be used to resolve the Kosovo crisis and that no one had any knowledge of. And another example is when Maslarovic, Markovic, and myself worked together, because my memory is now being refreshed and I can perhaps go back to the previous question as regards our cooperation. Everything Mr. Mihajlovic says is right. I could have read that in the papers, but in 2004, whereas I spoke about it in 1999 and 2000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said that. Try and answer -- just make the point just once, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just go back to the question pertaining to Maslarovic, Markovic, and myself, I didn't recall that at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the three of us worked together, although we never sat at the same table, but nevertheless were in the same room. When there was discussion about Monsignor Paglia's involvement as one of the negotiators and as someone that could be accepted by Milosevic. You can find this information in the book published by Predrag Simic, who was President Kostunica's advisor. You can clearly see there that Maslarovic and myself, and some other people secured Monsignor Paglia's involvement. Mr. Markovic participated in it as well. That was the first occasion we worked together, although we were not sitting down at the same table, but we were walking around. I apologise for this digression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where did that occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Italian embassy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think in 1995. Again, I would have to consult the notes and the book. It is in the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you refer to a book by Simic, who was advisor to which person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic also participated in the negotiations. At that time, he was director of the institute for strategic research. At that time, that was in 1998 or 1999. However, at the time, when he wrote the book, he was about to become President Kostunica's advisor. He wrote a book about Kosovo where he clearly states that I was involved in the negotiations. Simic was involved as an expert, and he also mentioned Maslarovic, myself. And he clearly states that Maslarovic and I helped the whole thing. And he also mentions Milutinovic's involvement and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have another question about this, the broadcast of the Mihajlovic interview. The television clip that you were shown in court during the Milosevic trial, and which I just read to you, it was broadcast on the evening of the 15th of May. And the next day in court, on the 16th of May, 2002, Exhibit 1D28, page 5108, you were asked: "Do you know about that statement that he made last night that we were able to hear live via Television Belgrade?" And your answer is: "Yes -- well, yes, I do. I know about it." Now, were you able to watch the statement by Mr. Mihajlovic on television? Did you see it on television on the evening of the 15th?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see it on television, but I spoke to a few members of my family who are in Serbia, and I was being denounced there, and they told me, Well, this is your boss talking about you this way. And since you are trying to present newspaper articles, perhaps you can also state here that Mr. Mihajlovic, some two or three months after my testimony in the Vreme magazine in an interview, which was conducted with me and Mihajlovic, he said that what I said was 90 percent true. So this is quite a different estimate, if you put it against this statement. So if you are going to put this interview to me, I [as interpreted] have another one to counter it. He said it plainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, you may not have any information on this, but it's a quite extraordinary coincidence that this should be broadcast immediately before cross-examination of the witness in the Milosevic trial. What channel did you say it was broadcast on?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My information it was on RTS television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a Belgrade -- that's Radio Television Serbia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, one correction for the transcript. On page 14, line 20, I think the witness said, Since you are showing this interview to me, we have another one to counter it, whereas in the transcript it says, "I have another one." I believe the distinction to be important. My learned friend Mr. Petrovic says that the witness probably meant the OTP as well. Perhaps we could check that against the audio recording.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need. I just asked the Prosecutor to put forth the interview, if they have it in their possession, the interview from Vreme. And when I said that "we have the interview," I meant I and the OTP. There is lots of material, lots of interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: One last point on this. When Mr. Mihajlovic gave in interview in May 2002, he was the Minister of the Interior, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And at that point Mr. Kostunica was president and Mr. Djindjic was prime minister, right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a different topic now, and I refer to your statement at paragraph 108. And here's what you say at paragraph 108, and I'll read it to you and then I'll ask some questions is about it. Paragraph 108 says: "During the NATO bombing, I had a heated conversation with Milosevic at a small reception. I had just returned from abroad" --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Which line of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Oh, excuse me. Yeah, I'm sorry, paragraph 108 --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which item?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see this in the B/C/S, as you call it, meaning Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, we'll use the English then. I'm at paragraph -- in English it's page 27, paragraph 108, and I'm reading the -- from the second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's the third sentence, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Third sentence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your statement says this: "During the NATO bombing I had a heated conversation with Milosevic at a small reception. I had just returned from abroad, where the SDB and Milosevic -- and Milosevic's approval." Sorry. "I just returned from abroad where with SDB and Milosevic's approval, I had been attempting to negotiate with foreign contacts an honourable way out of the crisis. I had passed on a discreet offer from Milosevic and had not received a response. Milosevic had lost control and stated that I was stupid, that I did not understand their strategy. He said,"We need to have enough civilian victims, because then when there are a lot of civilian casualties there, NATO countries' public opinion will tell their leaders to go to hell, and that is how we can defeat NATO." Now, this is what you told the Prosecutor in your interview. And when you met the Prosecutor this year on the 4th and 5th of November, 2000, you did not make any corrections or changes to your statement, did you? Sorry, 2006 you met the Prosecutor, just a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, let me remind you how you describe this event in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic. It's 1D27, 15th of May, 2002, pages 5007. It begins, and this is direct examination. Mr. Nice asks you this question: "In light of your willingness to give evidence publicly, are you willing now to tell us what happened at the April -- at the meeting in April 1999 with the accused, just yes or no. No explanation is required." "A. Yes. But with a correction as to the description. The description does not correspond entirely. That's probably my fault in this."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you intend with this? Are you about to ask me something or are you explaining to me that I -- you can see that I went abroad for negotiations in the archives of the State Security Service and as well as the other things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just wait and a question will be -- no question has been asked yet. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I was just pausing to let the interpreters catch up.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The question from Mr. Nice continues on page 5008, line 4, where he says: "Mr. Tanic, it may be that this background will be helpful. Our immediate interest is what the accused said to you at a face-to-face meeting or a face-to-face encounter, however you describe it. If you can move there very swiftly and then answer His Honour Judge Kwon's or my inquiry with your evidence, please. "A. Well, that's what it's about. As we did not have a face-to-face meeting, there was a telephone conference -- actually, and I'll take upon myself the responsibility. But I wasn't going to go into that but some other matters, and perhaps I did not devote attention to that. There was a personal telephone conversation, but not face-to-face, not a face-to-face encounter. "Q. What was said? "A. What was said that -- well, quite simply, there would be no cease-fire in the conflict for some time to come, that Serbia and Yugoslavia needed some more civilian victims. This was said on insistence to bring the war conflict to an end as soon as possible, but nothing -- I don't wish to say anything else about that because there she other traces of that accusation against Mr. Milosevic. "Q. Who said that? Who was at the other end of the telephone? "A. In order to prove that NATO was a criminal organisation, at the end of the previous paragraph, communication between Mr. Milosevic and Draskovic. I heard that on the speaker-phone. It was a reception, but it was our reception. Now, may I explain the context of it, if the Tribunal wishes to hear it, because the context is highly significant." Now, Mr. Tanic, you went from saying that you had a heated conversation with Milosevic at a small reception to saying that you overheard a speaker-phone conversation between Draskovic and Milosevic. Those two things don't add up, do they?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, may I comment this very precisely to be as of much use to the Court as possible. First of all, let me remind you that Mr. Milosevic is not here. This is not a trial against Milosevic, but I do understand your intentions. As you know, that trial was very difficult. There was a lot of fighting between the two of us, and I decided to testify it -- only on those facts that may be corroborated by other independent sources and it is stated in my statement as such. I chose another example that happened where other people could testify to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tanic, how often have I asked you to concentrate on the questions that are being asked and to direct your answer to the question. The question is inviting you to explain the quite marked difference between what you say in the statement at paragraph 108 and, if it's the same event, what you said in the Milosevic trial. Now, can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just answered that question, and I said that I would testify in court only about these things that can be corroborated. My direct conversations with Milosevic cannot be corroborated by anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop. Are you now refusing to answer the question? It's not for you to decide whether you'll answer on matters that can be corroborated; it's your job to answer every question that's put to you. Now, I ask you, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what was the question, whether I had two meetings with him? One conversation with him, direct conversation? I can say whatever I wish, because that man is no longer alive. Excuse me, but this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We may then decide that that's a third version, which would rather undermine your evidence. Are you not interested in trying to help us to reach a resolution of this and clarify what seems to be a contradiction? If you're not, we'll either move on; or, if I'm asked to, I will order you to answer the question. But Mr. O'Sullivan may be quite content to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that I answered this question. If there is anything else which is still unclear, I'm happy to clarify them. I think that I've explained this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give us a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tanic, Mr. O'Sullivan, we consider that Mr. Tanic has failed to answer that question. It's a matter for you now, Mr. O'Sullivan, how you proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, the portion I just read to you from the Milosevic transcript in 1D27, that was a direct examination of you by the Prosecutor. Exhibit 1D29 on the 21st of May, 2002, is your cross-examination on this point, the point being the difference between saying "I had a heated conversation with Milosevic at a reception," in your statement, and your testimony that you overheard the conversation between Milosevic and Draskovic on a speaker-phone. And at page 5186 you were asked this question: "All right. All right, Mr. Tanic. Do you know about Vuk Draskovic's statement precisely with respect to what you have just told us? And it says the following, and it was by Blic, the Belgrade daily newspaper: "The man denied in the course of the meeting with Mihajlovic that Milosevic was ever on a direct telephone line, and he assesses Tanic's statement as a complete untruth." "Now, is Vuk Draskovic speaking untruth as well, Mr. Tanic, is that it?" And your answer is: "Well, it's quite obvious now that everybody is washing their hands of it." Now, isn't it true that the reason people wash their hands of you is that you fabricate stories about yourself and others?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We apologise, but the English booth doesn't have any sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just stop a moment, Mr. Tanic. Apparently there is no sound going through to the English booth. Could you start that answer again please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid I'll need to ask you to stop. Apparently there is a technical problem, and there is no sound relaying to the English booth to translate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It should be okay now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that, Mr. Tanic. The matter has now been resolved. I have to ask you, I regret, to start that answer again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is very clear about Vuk Draskovic having taken part in all that, and there are other witnesses to that. And as far as them washing their hands, I said that they're washing their hands of the other things, not of me. Of course, everyone bears a certain portion of responsibility for the war not ending sooner. Some people were more to blame or less. Milosevic took most of the blame. Of course, nobody in Serbia is going to support what I am testifying about here, because it's not just about the war -- crimes against Kosovo Albanians, but about the betrayal of Serbia. Of course, Milosevic regime perpetrated crimes not only against Albanians, but also Serbians, and this is why I'm in the witness protection programme and my testimony is quite clear. It can be corroborated, and there are at least two or three witnesses as to witness Milosevic's strategy to rack up the number of civilian victims to stave off NATO attacks, but nobody else is going to incriminate him on that but me.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, at page 6398 of the transcript, you were asked this question: "In regard to that, did you have - now I'm talking about paragraphs 108 and 117 and 118 - during the course of the NATO bombing, did you personally have any conversation with Mr. Milosevic about the bombing and about civilian casualties, Serb civilian casualties?" . And your answer was: "It was a brief conversation. I cannot be specific as to its detail, but I remember him saying we needed civilian casualties to justify everything. He's dead now, and there was some other people who were present. It is a state secret, and it's up to this Tribunal to assess the truthfulness of everything I say." That's a third version of that event, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that the gist of it is the same. And you know in war times, I cannot really describe all the circumstances in great detail, because in that case no witness protection programme could save me. I cannot push people to their own death by citing that they were there, and I cannot really condemn my family to death by picking a fight with several countries. You know, this is a chaotic situation, wartime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, please get real. In -- you are being asked for your recollection of events; you're not being asked for other people's recollections. You're not being asked to name any other individuals who were present on this occasion. At this stage, you are simply being asked to explain accurately what happened. And you are persisting in refusing to address the apparent contradictions in the various explanations you've given. That leaves a Court -- remember, we are not politicians, we are not newspapers, we are not gossips in the street. We are a Court, and Courts operate on facts. And if you won't assist us by giving us the facts, then we will not be able to do justice. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like to change topics.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, may -- it is now clear, my position. Can I try to help the Court finally to resolve this contradiction? There was a conversation over the telephone and tete-a-tete, both occurred. But in no case can I corroborate that, verify that, or mention the circumstances in which they happened. With regard to the telephone conversation, I can say that it did take place. And all these variants are irrelevant because the gist of the conversation is the same. I'm trying to be helpful here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm moving on, Mr. Tanic. And I'm directing your attention to paragraph 125 of your statement. And I'll read from the second-last paragraph of -- second-last sentence of paragraph 125. You said this: "When the cease-fire did not begin on Catholic Easter and the three American soldiers were not released, I called Milutinovic on the phone and asked why the delay. He said, 'We have not finished the job. We will proclaim this unilateral cease-fire but we need another couple of days.'" Now, when you met the Prosecutor on the 4th and 5th of November, 2006, you changed your story, and you said this: "When the cease-fire did not begin on Catholic Easter and the three American soldiers were not released, I called Milutinovic on the phone and told him that Mihajlovic wanted to talk to him about the delay. He said, 'We have not finished the job. We will proclaim this unilateral cease-fire, but we need another couple of days.' When I got Mihajlovic on the phone, Milutinovic repeated to him that they needed time to finish the job." Now, when you testified in Milosevic, 1D27 is the exhibit, 15th of May, 2002, you said that you overheard a conversation between Milutinovic and Mihajlovic on a speaker-phone. Yesterday, you gave a fourth version, page 6403 of our transcript. You said that Mihajlovic was in his office when he called Milutinovic. You say Mihajlovic used a special phone to call Milutinovic. Milutinovic was in a secret command post, and Milutinovic said that the unfinished business down there -- that there was unfinished business down there and that it, the cease-fire, would happen on Orthodox Easter. Well, sir, on four different occasions you've given four different accounts of this story. None of it adds up, does it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The gist is the same. But it's true that it's a bit confused, because I do not have very precise recollection -- well, it took us quite a while to find him. It was wartime, you know, and this is why confusion created. I corrected that in my talks with the Prosecution, and the gist was the same that Milutinovic that we had not finished the job. The gist of the conversation is the same. Of course, it is depicted in a confused manner as to the circumstances. I do have this kind of problem because many events happened and some of them bear emotionally on me. In my statement, the gist is never changed; circumstances are described differently. This is of course due to my memory, which works under the burden of hundreds of events stored there.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, in 1999, Mr. Mihajlovic was not in government, was he?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mihajlovic was always one of the most influential politicians in Serbia, whether in government or outside of government. And in his cabinet --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir. Sir, I'm not disputing whether he was a politician or not. I said in 1999, Mr. Mihajlovic was not in government. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I didn't say he was a politician; I said that he was a very influential politician. Now you are offering three or four different versions. I have to respond to confused -- well, you're presenting your case in a very calm situation, in a courtroom. You do not have to worry about your life, and I'm ostensibly guilty of not recollecting some technical, minor details. But my -- the gist and the [indiscernible] is the same. I said he was one of the most influential politicians in Serbia, be it outside the government or in the government. But he was not in the government, but he had maintained all of his contacts and he placed great hope in Milutinovic and in all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you know whatever happened with the unilateral cease-fire declared by the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The offer to shorten the war was not implemented in the form that I related, and therefore bombing increased and continued. Kumanovo capitulation occurred without a possibility to maintain the Pristina Corps where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at tab 5 is Exhibit 1D37, and I direct the Court's attention to it. You'll see that it's a document from the internet with the web site appearing at the top of the document, and it indicates that in 1999, western Easter was the 4th of April and Orthodox Easter was the 11th of April. And I'd like to make an oral application to have the Court take judicial notice of those dates under Rule 94(A).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I currently don't have any reason to dispute that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That application is granted, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like then to move to Exhibit 1D36, which is at tab 6. That's a joint statement of the Federal Government and the Government of the Republic of Serbia, dated the 6th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I direct everyone's attention to paragraph 1, which states that: "In the observance of the greatest Christian holiday, Easter, as of 6th April 1999, at 8.00 p.m., all activities of the army and police in Kosovo against the terrorist organisation KLA cease unilaterally." And I won't read the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you see, Mr. Tanic, that on Tuesday, the 6th of April, there was in fact a unilateral cease-fire, contrary to what you've just said; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I object to the form of the question because Catholic Easter is shown as being on the 4th. The 6th is two days after the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I believe he said there was no cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the 4th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I apologise. Please. This is the end. I said that there was no cease-fire in the way that it was agreed upon. There was some cease-fire. It was half-baked and in the best manner of Milosevic's regime, but I stated that the cease-fire did not take place in the form as agreed. I would like to -- the Bench to protect me from these implications from the Defence, and this is illegal and immoral. I apologise to the Bench and the Prosecution and everybody in the courtroom, but I cannot really allow the Defence to imputations. The semantic difference is between Serbian and English, a phrase I never uttered. They are accusing me of giving contradictory statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you are unduly defensive about something that carries no imputation against you whatsoever, other than the suggestion that you are fabricating your evidence. The point that is being made to you is that the cease-fire did not take place on the Orthodox Easter, which was the 11th of April. And as a piece of evidence in support of that proposition, it's being put to you that there was a statement, a press statement -- or a statement issued on the 6th of April. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the transcript says the point that is being made to you is that the cease-fire did not take place on Orthodox Easter, which was the 11th. I thought the point was being made that the cease-fire did not take place on the 4th of April, which was Catholic Easter, as opposed to Orthodox Easter. Maybe I misunderstand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, you're quite right, Mr. Hannis. It's my misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Except for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from that, this is just a statement. It wasn't implemented immediately. They waited for one or two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, indeed that sounds like a sensible sort of answer to make to the question you're being asked, if you would apply your mind to the questions. But I apologise for misleading you to the extent I have by referring to the Orthodox Easter instead of Catholic Easter. Mr. O'Sullivan, Mr. Hannis makes the point that all this document does is confirm that the cease-fire didn't take place at the Catholic Easter.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Then I asked Mr. Tanic if he knew whether a cease-fire ever occurred, and I just put this document to show him that there was a joint statement of two levels of government. I don't dispute the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a question for you, Mr. Tanic. Was there a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cease-fire did not occur on the Catholic Easter, as was agreed, neither did it occur in its entirety, as had been agreed. I'd like to ask if I was not involved in all that, how could I have known about this highly confidential piece of information on the end of the war, on Catholic Easter, if I had not been involved in negotiations? Nobody else knew that this was going on. What are we talking about? And there's another thing that I would like to comment in this statement, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, I'd be grateful if you would answer the question, which is: Was there actually a cease-fire? Never mind the date, just tell us if there was a cease-fire at any stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was, but not in the manner that had been agreed. Withdrawal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the question. There was. Now, tell us what the difference was between what was anticipated and what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wasn't out on the ground at that time. As far as I received information, the political agreement was problematic again, because one of the component parts of the peace offer by NATO was a political agreement. And I believe that this was a bone of contention, and the withdrawal -- and this is why NATO continued with this intervention. But I must tell you that I wasn't there on the ground, and I do not have first-rate information about events there. I believe that there were some problems connected with political solution for Kosovo more than affecting the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not the issue at the moment, I don't think, Mr. Tanic. You've said that there was a cease-fire but that it wasn't implemented in the way envisaged. What we would like to know is what actually happened and what was different about that from what had been anticipated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It -- the cease-fire was partial. The withdrawal started, but a partial one, not a complete withdrawal. The political agreement was not concluded. I believe that Milosevic and his people would sign anything but never implement anything, and had they implemented all they signed, Milosevic would have received a Nobel Peace Prize. But the problem is they never observed their own agreements. The cease-fire was partial; it was not complete. And the withdrawal was partial and not complete. But now I'm treading on the ground where I do not have complete information and I could not comment on the whole. Some fighting did continue. Of course the KLA used this opportunity to abuse the situation. And since everything was being done underhanded and many members of the military and police never knew about this peace agreement, they were flabbergasted they were being withdrawn. Milosevic manipulated both the military and the police as well. So chaos reigned around this agreement and it was not implemented in the way envisaged. Of course I do not know all the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, may I interrupt for a moment. I just want to put my record -- on the record my objection to this exhibit at this point in time without some further foundation. It's not signed or sealed. It does have a fax header indicating 6th of April, 1999, from the YUFMFA -- perhaps that's the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Office, but to a particular phone number. I have no more information about it to determine whether or not this was official, whether it was approved, whether it was a draft, or anything else. So I object to it for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're in the process of working with the Prosecution on stipulations, and I'm confident that we can come to an agreement on this one; if not, we'll deal with it in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Hannis, when a document like this is used by the Defence, our practice will be to admit it as an exhibit. But that doesn't prove anything. It simply puts in context the evidence that the witness gave, unless there is some recognition, for example, as has happened with Prosecution exhibits which are witness statements, that it's being accepted in its entirety as a document for consideration. So that's what would happen to this one. And you having particularly made the point, then the Defence are clearly on notice that they have to establish a basis for regarding this as authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like to change topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, could you confirm for us that Vuk Draskovic's political party was called the Serbian Renewal Party.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I repeat my question again: How could I have known about this proposal had I not been involved. I couldn't have read it in the papers. Just to remind you --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, I've moved on. I'm changing topics.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly you did. I know you did. I can see that. You changed topics. Yes, the Serbian Renewal Movement is Vuk Draskovic's party.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to direct your mind to the National Assembly of Serbia on the 23rd of March, 1999, and the Assembly session that was held on that date. Did -- did Vuk Draskovic address the Assembly on the 23rd of March, 1999, the Serbian Assembly; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to be allowed to consult the notes. Do you have this among the papers given?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, maybe -- this may refresh your memory, and you can tell me if it does. 1D27 is the Milosevic transcript of the 15th of May, 2002, and in that portion of the transcript you're talking about individuals who addressed the Assembly --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we have a page reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You've said that -- by this point in the transcript you said that Mr. Milutinovic had addressed the Assembly. And Mr. Nice asks you: "Did Vuk Draskovic provide an alternative?" And you said: "To the best of my knowledge, yes, he did, on behalf of a group of people who compiled an alternative solution to the Serbian Assembly which should have been sufficient to avoid this conflict with the NATO pact, which would have been suicidal." Now, it's unclear to me whether you're saying that Mr. Draskovic addressed the Assembly or whether he didn't. If you don't know, that's fine; if you do know, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Please, Mr. O'Sullivan. Let's drop semantics. Of course he addressed the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a public document. As far as I can recall, he addressed the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you -- were you present at the Assembly that day? Did you watch it on television? Do you have a recollection of Mr. Draskovic addressing the Assembly? Just tell us.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I've read the minutes from that Assembly session pertaining to Milutinovic. I didn't pay much attention to Draskovic's words because I was interested in what Milutinovic would say, since Holbrooke was outside the door; he was waiting for the Assembly's decision. And you can see all that from the official minutes of the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the official minutes. It's 1D32, tab 9 in hard copy. It's a rather lengthy document, but both the English and the B/C/S are in hard copy. You can see from the cover page that it's the shorthand minutes of the 1st Session of the first regular sitting of the Republic of Serbia National Assembly, 23 March 1999. If you turn to the next page, contents, it's the report of the state delegation on talks in Rambouillet and Paris. And then you can see that the session begins with the Speaker Dragan Tomic opening the session. Now, if we go to page 60 of the English and page 79 of the B/C/S, page 60 in English and page 79 in B/C/S -- have you got that page, Mr. Tanic? Page 79 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You have an index of the speakers. The name Vuk Draskovic doesn't appear there, does it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Where do you see it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it, but we were not discussing Draskovic, we were discussing Milutinovic's speech at the Assembly. So what is this issue of Draskovic? He's not in the index of speakers. Maybe he didn't address the Assembly. I may have been mistaken as well. When -- once I found out that the thing fell through, well, I wanted to see what Milutinovic would say because everything depended on his words, whether there would be peace or war. I wasn't interested in Draskovic anymore. When I had learned overnight that the thing fell through, I wanted to follow the session and to pay attention to Milutinovic's words. I wasn't interested in whether Draskovic addressed the Assembly or not. You should try and read out Milutinovic's speech. This is what I addressed in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: A moment ago I asked you if you knew that Mr. Draskovic spoke in the Assembly. You said, Yes, he did. And here we see that the minutes indicate that Mr. Draskovic did not. Do you understand my point?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I know what you're trying to do. You're trying to capitalise on the gaps in my memory. I understand it perfectly well; that's why I'm in good humour. Please, go ahead, continue with your technical tricks, but please touch upon the essence for once. And I'm trying to ask you kindly as a witness. You approached the essence once when discussing the Easter agreement, and then you moved on after I asked you, How could I have known about it? Therefore, yes, I apologise. I was mistaken. It seems Vuk Draskovic was not at the session, and I paid attention only to Milutinovic's speech, since it was decisive. It was to decide whether there would be war or peace. I apologise to the Bench, to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have a different question. Sir, are you aware that the Rambouillet agreement never contemplated troops in Kosovo under the UN flag or with a mandate from the UN Security Council? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank God, finally I get a specific question as regards the essence. That is not true. The draft agreement did not foresee the troops to be under the UN flag. But later on, during the negotiations - as can be confirmed by Milutinovic and other witnesses - there was a possibility left to Serbia to accept NATO troops' presence under the UN flag; therefore, that the agreement be changed. Finally you get to the point, and I'd suggest that you exercise caution because there are many witnesses as to the contents. I categorically state that the Serbian delegation, as early as Rambouillet and afterwards, was offered the possibility to amend or change the unfavourable NATO mandate in our terms and to put it under the UN flag and the auspices of the Security Council. There was that possibility as well as the possibility of a favourable peaceful political solution, as was affirmed by Milutinovic partially in his address. The international community wanted to see peace troops there in any which way possible, so they were not focusing on one thing or the other [as interpreted]. But I do agree with you: The initial draft did not foresee any NATO troops, but that was left open for the negotiations and the dialogue. It would have -- well, when Markovic went to Rambouillet, they laughed at it, but subsequently when Milutinovic took part, things got better. But of course he had to stick by our -- with Milosevic's ideas and wish to create war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a problem -- there is a problem with the transcript. Maybe the -- maybe the witness should be really guided to speak slower because I assume that the interpreters cannot follow the pace at what he is speaking. Because the -- it's 36, 24: "The international community wanted to see peace troops there in any which way possible, so they were not focusing on one thing or the other." The witness said quite a different thing about the NATO troops and all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell me what he said?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he said the international community wanted to see peace troops there, insisted on NATO the first time, but then -- I don't remember it quite -- quite the words because I was concentrating on some other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Tanic, tell us again -- just hold on. Tell us again what you say the international community wanted to see in the way of peace troops.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The international community wanted to see peace troops in Kosovo, which would guarantee the implementation of the political agreement as well as to guarantee that there would be no further conflict. There was a possibility left to negotiate as to the flag, whether it -- that would be the UN's flag and the Security Council's auspices. There was a possibility left for the Serbian side, provided they are cooperative, that even the Pristina Corps would remain down there to cooperate, to some extent, with the UN troops. I categorically state that this is true, and one can have at least a dozen of witnesses which would corroborate that, and Milutinovic himself has to confirm as well. As for the possible changes to our benefit, to have the UN flag and the Pristina Corps there, that was all under the caveat that peace troops are accepted. We could even have gained a pretty good political agreement which would be more in favour of Serbs than of Albanians. Milutinovic can confirm this as well. But Milosevic said, I don't want any troops. That was his excuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tanic. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I'll try this question. Sir, I put it to you that the Rambouillet agreement and the Rambouillet and Paris process only contemplated NATO forces in the FRY, not pursuant to a UN Security Council Resolution; it was NATO and NATO only, Russia, a permanent member of the Security Council, did not support implementation of Rambouillet, and that's why it was NATO and only NATO. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. And this attorney-at-law is not qualified and does not have the expertise to interpret complicated political arrangements. It's simply incorrect. I wasn't going into armed forces technicalities. Could the counsel please be asked not to meddle with high politics and agreements. It is incorrect. The answer is no. There was a possibility. The initial draft from Rambouillet foresaw NATO presence, but during negotiations you can try and change that. As for Milutinovic, he could have said, Yes, we will accept such troops under the UN flag and the Security Council's auspices. Milutinovic may have opted for that, but Milosevic said, No troops, because he saw the possibility to create war in that, and he needed it. And therefore, we were not able to accept that. Had we accepted the UN flag, we could have participated as well, being a member. As regards the rest, you can call at least five or ten credible witnesses here of much higher rank than of Milutinovic or Tadic, and then you'll see. They simply lied about Rambouillet. They lied before that, but they lied after it as well, Milosevic and his associates. Milosevic met with Madeleine Albright on several occasions, but no option was found for the troops to move about the territory. The offer made was to stay in their bases, but what would be their use then? Mr. Milutinovic was in a difficult situation. I understand him. He was an experienced diplomat, and I don't think this was his view, but he chose to obey by Milosevic's ideas and orders. Milosevic welcomed any excuse to start a war in Kosovo, and he used his associates to lie or to misinterpret Rambouillet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, we're now wandering through areas which are not the subject of this question. Mr. O'Sullivan, do you have a while to go yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: A little while, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you saw how Mr. Hannis approached this, and I appreciate the importance to you, but I hope the overall timing is being borne in mind in dealing with the witness. We now have to break, Mr. Tanic. If -- we'll go into closed session for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, do you know of a man named Spasoje Krunic, who was a member of the Serbian Renewal Party? Have you ever heard of him?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- well, I think I've heard of his name, but -- well, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. You've heard of him?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Did you know that he was a member of a five-person commission which was set up to draft conclusions of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia on the 23rd of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Such details were of no interest to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record it's Exhibit 1D32, which are the minutes of the Assembly, page 12. That's my reference to -- for my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this a reference to a document prior to the actual Assembly discussion?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No. Page -- I'm looking at page 12 of the actual minutes, during which the Speaker, Mr. Tomic, after the presentation by Mr. Markovic, the report of Mr. Markovic, relating to Rambouillet in Paris, he establishes a five-person commission, including Mr. Krunic, to draft the ultimate conclusions of the Serbian Assembly of that day, in relation to the report tabled by Professor Markovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any reference in these minutes to the document that it was said was compiled with the assistance of Draskovic and Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The conclusions are at the very end of this document. They begin -- the conclusions themselves begin at page 56 of the English version. So my reference to the five-person commission are the people responsible for actually drafts or presenting these conclusions which begin at page 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But the question I have is a rather different one about the witness's evidence that there was a proposal that was being submitted through the hand of Draskovic. Now, did that -- is there any reference to that proposal at all in the discussion?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, okay. I can read it obviously for myself, but I was just curious to speed up the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, in that same vein, what I propose to do is offer this complete set of minutes. It's at tab 10, it's 1D32, which include the speeches by the 28 people who spoke that day in the Assembly, including Mr. Milutinovic who spoke 12th. They also include the conclusions adopted by the Serbian Assembly on that day. In due course, I wish to deal with both the conclusions in comparison to P710, which are Draskovic's drafts; and also in due course I will deal what this witness has to say about Milutinovic's speech, based on the words he actually used. So if we can proceed in that way, I think it's the most economical way. I will just tender 1D32 in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know really how you can do that at this stage. You're suggesting that we should take account of this in due course as part of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No. "In due course," I mean when we come to final submissions. We have what the witness has said about Milutinovic's speech. I'm tendering the full Milutinovic speech in the context of all the interventions I've made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suspect the only way this can be done, in the context of the Prosecution case, is either by stipulation or through a witness that can actually say, "Yeah, these are the minutes of the meeting." And I suspect that this witness isn't in a position to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hannis can say whether he wants to stipulate it now or whether he wants to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm certainly not meaning to be awkward about this because I encourage this kind of approach, but we have to bear in mind what the Rules allow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's likely the kind of thing I'm willing to agree to. I just have to do some independent verification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you note the position and we'll see what develops.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, last week -- I'm changing topics now, Mr. Tanic. Last week you stated that someone from the British secret service was present during a part of your interviews with the OTP, and you explained that he was there for the sake of confirming the identity of the people at The Hague Tribunal and your identity, because you had not previously met. Do you recall saying that? Have I fairly summarised what you said?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as usual. I said that person was present to verify my identity and the identities of The Hague Tribunal representatives, since we didn't see each other before and we never met. He was there to say, "Yes, this is Ratomir Tanic." And he wasn't there throughout, but just at the beginning when the identities had been confirmed. Then the person withdrew and no longer participated in our conversation. There's something I wanted to correct in the transcript. The tangent I mentioned of Milutinovic offering bases for troops without their being able to move, but perhaps we can also check that against the audio-recording. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, it's becoming quite tedious listening to you making allegations against counsel which don't seem to have any foundation. You've just confirmed that Mr. O'Sullivan's statement of the position was entirely accurate, 100 percent accurate. But you prefaced that by saying when he asked you had he fairly summarised what he said, "No, as usual." Now, I caution you to be very careful in the way in which you are responding to perfectly reasonable questions put by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, when you testified in the Slobodan Milosevic case - and this is Exhibit 1D27, 15th of May, 2002, pages 5029, 5030 - you gave a few more details in relation to the presence of the British secret service. And again I'll summarise what you said. You said that there were there to provide security to you, because they had established that you were the victim of torture, perhaps even attempted murder, together with your wife. Do you recall saying that, and is that a fair summary of what you said?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was an additional reason. There were several, and this was something that was an addition to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I believe you said a moment ago, and it was put to you by Mr. Hannis, that the British secret service agent was present during the first and perhaps the second session of your interview with the OTP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can describe this person. He was there but in a different room.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tanic, there's a problem with your --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have problems with interpretation again. [Microphone not activated] I didn't say I can describe this person. I said that I can describe the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's quite all right. I have a basis for my next question, because you see there's a problem with your story. The problem is that the first couple of days of your interview with the OTP were on the 21st of June and the 22nd of July, 1999. And we see that from the cover page of your statement, where the first two days of the interview occur on those two dates I told you. And the problem is this: You claim you were kidnapped in October 1999, and it would have been impossible for the British secret service to provide security because of kidnapping and torture; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is creating confusion because if you look at the transcript on page 5029 at the bottom the witness says: "I'm not testifying here on general political matters but very specific secrets which your regime tired to hush up and they are providing protection for me, I assume. Because with all their check-outs that they have done, they have established that I was at least the victim of torture, perhaps even attempted murder." He's referring to at the time he's testifying about the protection that's being offered to him. He wasn't saying that he was being protected in June and July 1999 because he'd been kidnapped; he was refer to at the time he was testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In the Milosevic -- sir, you accept that you've told this Court in the Milosevic trial that you were kidnapped from the street in October 1999. That's the story you've told the Milosevic Trial Chamber, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct. And I agreed that I wasn't in June and July victim of kidnapping, but a person from the British security service was there for several reasons; first to verify my identity and then at meetings regarding protection. And then my meetings with the Prosecution in June/July were of courteous nature. We did discuss things, but my real official statement was given to the OTP in 2000. And in June and July 1999 Brussels, we discussed the same things, these things, in the same manner, but generally in terms of exchange of opinions and clarifying certain problems. But in my first official statement to The Hague investigators, dates at the beginning of 2000 after my wife and I had been kidnapped and tortured.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the -- there's a matter of dispute again, that's for argumentation later. My reference to this is his testimony -- this witness's testimony in our case; 1D27, 15th of May, 2002, in the Milosevic case; and I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: When you testified in Milosevic, again on the 15th of May, 2002, 1D27, beginning at pages 4979, you say you were kidnapped off the street, injected, beat, suffocated. And you say your wife was not drugged, but she was beaten. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing that she received tranquillizer injection when we were kidnapped. We received some jabs during that torture. She did not receive jabs during torture; I did. These were vitamin jabs to perk me up during torture. She did not receive any jabs during torture, but she did receive a tranquillizer injection during the actual kidnapping. The rest is accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But did you see her receiving any kind of tranquillizers or injections during the time that you were both held, your wife? Did you see this being done to her?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were kept in separate rooms. She later told me that she had not received any injections during torture and the beatings. And I know that I received them, and I knew that they were very strong vitamin jabs to perk me up. And I knew them by their effect because I was very badly beaten, but we were kept in separate rooms, you know, in a private prison, not in a regular prison. And this is confirmed in a book by a high official of State Security Service. He said that the JSO units had kidnapped us, and this is beyond contention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And not State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
