utterances.text: So that I've understood, you and your wife were taken to what you call a private prison in the same location, but kept in separate rooms. Is that a fair description?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, that's interesting because at page 4981 of the Milosevic transcript you say: "We were both kidnapped, drugged, and taken to two different private prisons, where we spent two days each, my wife and myself, that is." Another fabrication, right, Mr. Tanic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, God. You're an impossible person, man. It says we were both kidnapped. Of course, I first and then one and a half hours later she. And we were taken to both separate prisons -- well, you are hanging on to every interpunction. I probably was in the same prison with different rooms. How could I have known because I was wearing a Balaclava? I was beaten up; I was drugged. How could I know where my wife was at the time? Please, man, trying to imputate that I fabricated facts. You have confirmation from the second in command of the State Security Service that this had happened. Of course, he described different circumstances, but he did say these were the JSO people, the same people who tried to -- Vuk Draskovic, who had killed Ivan Stambolic. Man, please do not play around with people's fates and destinies.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Another fabrication, right, Mr. Tanic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of a question is that, Mr. O'Sullivan? I would like to see you in that position, and I would have liked to have seen your reaction and would have liked to have seen you then being told that you had fabricated that. And anyway, one of the highest officials confirmed this; and of course this is true as the rest of my testimony. And of course I don't know where my wife was. Maybe she was in the room next door, maybe in a different prison. How could I have known when I was being choked, beaten up, forced to admit about a coup d'etat by Perisic, Mihajlovic, et cetera. They are asking me about British intelligence. Have you ever had been beaten this much that you can still feel the consequences?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My next question is what you say at page 4983 of the Milosevic transcript. You say that the people that kidnapped you and took you away and tortured you were actually people who wanted you to link them up with the British intelligence service so that they could topple Mr. Milosevic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, after the torture they played this game. If they couldn't get what they wanted by beating me, then they tried to be cagey. And they said that they wanted to link up with the British intelligence service, to carry out a coup d'etat against Milosevic, which was a very cagey story. Because there were in some quarters in Belgrade the school of thought that a coup d'etat had to be carried out against Milosevic to save the country. There was thoughts to that effect but no actions, and this was a cagey trick on their behalf. Later on I saw those people did take part in another story, but -- a deal with the Djindjic government, but this is not the subject matter of this trial. Of course after beating me and not obtaining any evidence from me into a video camera against Perisic, Mihajlovic, and other people who were involved in the political life of Serbia, then they changed tack and tried to be cagey about it. We would like to contact the British, and you may help us, and I believe that this was a test to gauge what kind of pressure I could take. And this is a mechanism used by intelligence services, but this is obviously nothing that you'd know about, Mr. O'Sullivan. So first, they beat me up and then they started being cagey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I refer you and the Court to Mr. Tanic's statement, paragraph 98, and I won't read it to you, sir. You can look at it if you like. But there you gave an account of the kidnapping, and there's no mention of your wife at all, is there, in this account? It's paragraph 98.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. O'Sullivan, you should be ashamed. I don't want to produce a mellow drama out of my issues. I do not want to play the emotional notes. I did not mention my wife. And I am very laconic about my abduction. My wife turned grey overnight after the experience. A high official, Zoran Mijatovic, high official of secret service, and at the time he preparing [as interpreted] the materials for his book. He was deputy head of state security under new government, and he confirmed that my wife and I were kidnapped, that that was done by the units for special operations, JSO, that they started to put the jigsaw pieces together, that the same members of JSO were those who had assassinated Curuvija and Stambolic, had attempted to kill Vuk Draskovic, and this was one day, the Draskovic assassination attempt, one or two days after my kidnapping, and this has been a contributing fact to our getting out of prison. Of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, please concentrate. You've answered the question right at the beginning of that answer. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: A moment ago I read a portion of your testimony from the Milosevic case where you say the people who kidnapped you were those who wanted to topple Milosevic. It's also true that during the Milosevic testimony you blame Mr. Milosevic for your kidnapping and torture. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The only thing is that they wanted to topple Milosevic was a trick of theirs. So that if they couldn't drag information from me by beating, they tried to be cagey. They tried this ploy. They did want to topple him at the time, be sure, because they would have done so if they had wanted. So this was a ploy. And of course I accused Milosevic because that unit operated under Milosevic's orders exclusively, and there are -- there is evidence to that from different sources. And Rade Markovic, head of the security service at the time when I was kidnapped, also confirmed that. And I was kidnapped together with my wife, I have to stress that once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You've mentioned a couple of times a book written by Mr. Mijatovic. That book was written in 2004, wasn't it? Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it is stated on the cover page. But it was being prepared when he was for the second time in row deputy head of state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Leave it to that because I just say that confirmation is contained in that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You can confirm that the date of publication of he book was 2004; correct? That's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And that's two years after you testified publicly in the Milosevic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let's go back to the British secret service. You received financial assistance from the British secret service, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the first time seven years after we had got to know each other, six or seven years after first contacts, I received financial support from the British intelligence service. I can describe that because I have been cleared to mention that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: How much did the British give you, how much money?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it weren't the British but representatives of British intelligence service, SAS, not British. We're not talking about Serbs or British. So the total amount was approximately -- I believe that I said that in my testimony in the Milosevic case. You can refer to that. I believe that it was 10.000 German marks, today's counter value of 5.000 euro, for the expenses connected with the preparation of different materials, the book, et cetera, and I could not have funded that out of my own pocket. That was in 1999. That was the first time that I received money from the British intelligence service, but we had contacts from 1992. We did not act against the interests of Serbia; we acted against Milosevic's regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The 5.000 euros you mentioned, how was that paid to you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, directly. Around 5.000 euro. You've got it in the transcript, and Mr. Nice asked me about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just answer the question. How was it paid to you? Cash? Cheque? What?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cash, in cash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's easy, you know, when you concentrate on the question. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So there's no receipt for this; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course there is no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So you were handed 5.000 euros; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the amount --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sorry. You were handed 10.000 Deutschemarks, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Was this -- all this money was in a bag or an envelope? But it was given to you personally in one instalment. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, on two occasions. And this isn't such a large quantity that a bag would be needed. And it was handed over to me on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Were you given any money on any other occasion by the British?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after I fled to Hungary, six months after that, a smaller amount. Of course I could not work in Hungary, could not find job at first, and I couldn't find a job at first in the Netherlands. So I received a smaller amount to buy food, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And how much was that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Does 4.000 to 6.000 Deutschemarks sound right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may consult the notes and transcripts from the Milosevic trial. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And after you left Yugoslavia in the fall of 1999, you were received by the Hungarian government and western intelligence agencies. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After they'd verified that I had really been kidnapped with my wife and that things had occurred in the specified way, their assessment was that it went for an attempted murder. And within that context, the Hungarian government and western intelligence services accepted me. After they'd verified the objective level of the threat to my life and the life of my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm moving to my last area of questions, sir, and I'm changing topics. Exhibit 1D28 is the Milosevic transcript of the 16th of May, and I'm on page 5106. I'm going to read to you an answer you gave to a question posed by Judge Kwon. And you said this: "I will clarify that very gladly. The accused, Mr. Milosevic, is denying everything, starting from my very existence all the way up to my role. My position is that during my testimony before this Court, I'm going to say only things that can be corroborated from two or three independent sources in addition." I'd like to read another short passage. 1D27, 15th of May, 2002, page 5025. I'm referring to lines 12 to 18. And you say this, I'll just read a portion of it: "I can always prove all my contacts from at least two or three independent sources." With the Court's indulgence, I'll read one short passage in addition and then I'll ask my question. The final portion I'd like to read to you, sir, is 1D28, Milosevic transcript from 16th of May, 2002, page 5092. You were asked this question. "Q. You claim in your written statement that you met me in the Deputies' Club secretly. "A. No, I didn't say that. I didn't say 'secretly.' I think that you were in the Deputies' Club on one occasion, but I threw out everything that I was not able to corroborate with independent sources, so that needn't be taken into account." Now, my question is: We see in this last portion of transcript that you withdrew a part of your statement that could not be corroborated by two or three independent sources; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I know that this Court is not satisfied with this position, but I dealt with politics and intelligence, and we always say things that can be corroborated by either two or three independent sources, both in politics and in intelligence work. This is my habit, my second nature. I know that this Court and this Chamber is not satisfied with the position the same way that the previous Chamber was not. I did withdraw all parts of my statements against Milosevic that could not be corroborated by two or three independent sources. He turned his trial into a circus act, and I didn't want to aggravate the position, neither of the Court nor of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, isn't it correct, sir, that this is exactly what the New Democracy press statement, Dusan Mihajlovic, and Vuk Draskovic say about your testimony, that it's nothing more than rumours, hearsay, and untruths. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not, because this is not verification from two or three sources. And when I say "verification," I don't mean reading newspaper articles. If they want -- and if you want -- if you want to verify that, you may call them to testify. But verification is not reading newspapers, neither in intelligence work or in judicial proceedings, neither in normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. I do, however, wish to tender the Milosevic transcript in its entirety, that's 1D26, 1D27, 1D28, and 1D29. I'm not tendering this testimony for the truth of its contents, but rather, to allow the Chamber to see the full context of this witness's testimony in the Milosevic case where he was cross-examined by the accused, Milosevic, who challenged him, his credibility in relation to all the meetings and contacts that he had with Mr. Milosevic. That transcript also contains the challenges made to him by other institutions and other people in Serbia. And I submit that it's appropriate for you to be able to evaluate this witness's testimony in the light of our cross-examination here and the full record of the Milosevic case, and it allows us also to tailor and streamline and reduce our cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Hannis, your comment on the use to which the transcript could be put at this stage insofar as it's not been specifically crossed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would -- I would urge you to admit the whole thing for all purposes that you deem fit. I was bothered by some of the brief references that were read because I think when they're just taken out of context like that, you may not have the full and complete understanding of them. And so I would urge -- I don't oppose its admission, and I would ask you to give whatever weight you deem fit for all purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't exist, Mr. O'Sullivan, as an exhibit with a number, I take it. I certainly wouldn't be insisting on it being produced in that form.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It is uploaded into our system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All four days in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what number does it have -- is it all 1D27?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will admit the transcript of the evidence of the witness in the Milosevic trial. That, of course, raises the possibility of the Court wishing to examine the witness and -- but that will always remain a possibility in a situation like this. It's unlikely we would be in a position to do so, however, during his current attendance here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For future reference, Your Honour, if the Court deems it appropriate and necessary to have him come back at a future date, we would only ask you to give us lots of notification because of his circumstances it takes us a while to make those arrangements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We appreciate that. Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Now, Mr. Fila, can I just before you start, say that I anticipate in your cross-examination a potential for debate and dialogue at high speed, which may cause interpretation difficulties. Since you are speaking the same language and also because of your style, which is to get into discussion sometimes, rather than to focus particular questions. Now I don't want to cramp your style, because it may be helpful to all of us. But I think in this instance you have to bear, particularly, in mind the need to focus the issues as briefly as possible and try to help the witness concentrate on particular points that you are interested in. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's try and agree, Mr. Tanic. Let us not be too hasty.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By all means, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: First of all, I don't intend to insult you, and that was not my intention yesterday, in case you misunderstood. I was quoting Mihajlovic. In any case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before -- just another matter, Mr. Fila, before we go any further. Like the less-than-entirely-proficient concert pianist, who has someone to turn the pages, it might be a good idea if someone beside you is alerted to the control of the microphone, because I can see the potential here for crossing over. So if that duty is in the hands of a competent assistant, I think that will greatly assist us. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Risking to appear incompetent in your eyes, I wanted to say a few words or questions about Rambouillet. You will agree with me that the negotiations in Rambouillet concerned Kosovo and not troops?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Let us not get into any semantic distinctions. Did you know that the Serb delegation expressed their views as to their readiness to accept any foreign troops in order to achieve a successful agreement in Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a certain point, that was mentioned, but then it was withdrawn. You know how it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's why I said let us just touch upon it. Did you know that the international community, as the key component for determining the situation and the position of Kosovo, tried to impose an agreement on the obligations to accept the results of the referendum on the fate of Kosovo, which was to happen in the future?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. And that that deadline of three years could have been prolonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. I guess you are familiar with it then. Yes. There were three years in question. Do you agree with me that Serbia could not accept that. It couldn't accept it then. It couldn't accept it now, such referendum results on the fate of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Since there were political games in place which were at our disposal to protect ourselves in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Fila please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question was: Had the referendum stayed in the provisions, it would have been unacceptable. But had it been done the way you mentioned, that it was changed, then it would have been accepted?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But then you get into the question on what the referendum would concern itself with.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you just repeat the "yes."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the interpreters to add "yes" to the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does that mean --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was a technical hitch with Mr. Fila's microphone. We lost sound for a moment. Could the question be repeated, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, could you repeat that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does that mean that Serbia was supposed to accept secession, if referendum was accepted and it would have been in favour of secession?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation would have been very complicated, but it was even more complicated with the war. And I can see you are an expert on the topic, and I'm glad to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, this microphone arrangement is not working. It's being left on and we have to do this properly. So can we have your assistant alerted to the need to switch the microphone on and off as necessary. It's very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. As regards the transcript, page 60, line 11. It is stated as question, whereas it was actually an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean the words, "Can you just repeat the yes"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It is fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you know that Mrs. Madeleine Albright, in front of the entire delegation of ours, before three negotiators and before the entire American delegation, stated that only NATO comes into picture to enter Yugoslavia. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. It doesn't mean anything. There is always pressure in negotiations, then leeway, and so on and so forth. You go a step back, a step forth; you know how things go. And besides, there were negotiations before Rambouillet, and I always thought Rambouillet to come too late, and that we were supposed to have signed an agreement with Albanians before that. Rambouillet was the last chance. And you're trying to focus it, whereas there were negotiations before this. The Holbrooke arrangement could have been put in place, and there would have been no need for Rambouillet, which was very difficult for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you know that Holbrooke on the 24th of March, 1999 - as far as I understood you were not in Yugoslavia on that day - but on that day, he brought a piece of paper. It was a take-it-or-leave-it offer. It was no offer to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Holbrooke never came with such a paper based on the principle of take it or leave it. He's not that type of negotiator. He always has a reserve solution, a spare in his pocket, and he always negotiated with Milosevic. I've never seen him come with such an offer; I've never heard of it. Of course, you are talking of 1999 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The 22nd of March, 1999, the day before the Assembly session. He came with a piece of paper containing an offer of take it or leave it, or the next day there will be bombing?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Incorrect. He had a spare option concerning the UN flag and the Security Council mandate. Should there be a need, we can call in expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, you do not agree with me, or do you? An entire war was needed for NATO to accept the UN flag. That's what I was trying to tell you.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, we didn't need the war at all. We could have completed things with the Albanians in 1997 and 1998. That's the essence of my testimony. We could have done away with their terrorism, as well, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you who the person was you mentioned from the SDB. You know which session you mean -- I mean.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which session do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you didn't want to name of the person from the SDB?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move into private session for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not willing to state their name in private session; otherwise, because that person is still at work and his life can be in danger. Several independent sources can confirmed that I had deals with them, and that is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you mentioned him in a private session, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there were several people there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Fila is interjecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It's not the person whose last name starts with an M?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. I will ask you about him, without mentioning the name. Did you know that he was tasked by the SDB for the Vracar [Realtime transcript read in error "Racak"] municipality?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've known him for 25 years. Certainly, for the Vracar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Racak?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard Vracak. Then it was an interpretation mistake; they wrote down "Racak."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know if the use of these initials is the -- is going to cause any difficulty when the name was previously referred to privately? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know. I don't know if the witness would have a position on that. And I guess I would remind the speakers to take a pause in between questions and answers. That seems to be causing difficulty for everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, I've raised the matter. If anyone wishes action taken, they should alert me to it. Oh, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a correction for the transcript. The municipality mentioned is Vracar, V-r-a-c-a-r. Since I interjected at the moment we were discussing open or closed session, I just wanted to say that in the Milosevic case the name of that witness was mentioned in open session on several occasions. Therefore, the mentioning of initials would cause no damage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would cause no damage because that person is not linked with anything that would result in the loss of life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which municipality are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The municipality is Vracar in Belgrade, one of the central municipalities in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did the gentleman, at a certain point, go to Kosovo in 1998, and did he spent the first half of 1999 there up until June?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who did you have contact with? The contact you mentioned you had on five or six occasions a week when he was absent, when he was in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another operative, as well as several other people; and occasionally, I saw him when he returned from Kosovo. I had known him for 25 years, and we are good friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You entered the service around 1980 or a bit earlier?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't enter the service; that would be an overstatement. I became a collaborator; and then you advance slowly, you are being trained, et cetera, et cetera. I was being trained to be a political security operative. It is standard technique employed everywhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, you became a collaborator, and then you were promoted. What did you exactly mean?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When did I say that exactly? Within the network of collaborators, I advanced. And at a certain point, I no longer needed to use my pseudonym because everyone knew it was me, but I never said I went beyond a collaborator's network. The first, initial things we did were completely irrelevant. It was described by Mr. Mijatovic in his statement. We had contacts with the foreign service, but it was in the 1980s. Of course, at first, I wasn't the star of the show. I simply advanced as a collaborator. In the last few years, my status was such that I no longer needed my pseudonym; everything went directly to the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Directly to whom?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the top of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is the top of the service?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you know that. At the time, the head of the Belgrade centre was the person - and this was the most important centre of the security service in Serbia - and this was Mr. Mijatovic; and then on to Mr. Stanisic, who was always man number two in our service.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I know this, but the Bench doesn't. So I wanted to -- you to state this.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course you do. You know them, as well as I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you worked as collaborator, was your pseudonym Rabin?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why can't you answer it? Are you surprised that I know it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not. Mijatovic mentioned it in his book. My favourite collaborator Rabin, meaning rabbi, is walking around with the Minister Mihajlovic in Paris having straws. You could have read that in the book, but I can't answer your question because I don't know what pseudonyms were used at that place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, what do you mean by describing Stanisic as "always man number two in our service"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another faulty interpretation. I mean Mr. Mijatovic. We have problems with interpretation, Your Honour. The only thing that would help would be if Mr. Fila and I need to abstain from exchange of opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zoran Mijatovic is number two and Jovica Stanisic would be number one. This is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I only need to be told once, normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: After Stanisic and Mijatovic left - and that would be October/November 1998 - who did you maintain contacts with?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There's a glitch in the microphone. Interpreter's note: The microphone of Mr. Fila was switched off again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer that because that person may be brought into trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is the second answer that you do not want to provide. Would you change your mind if we went into private session?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have mentioned this person's identity when they received the peace agreement, without commenting whether I had meetings with that person or not. This is what I can say in private session, because that person, as operative of the DB, received the peace agreement to shorten the war. I can mention that in private session without comment whether that person had worked with me or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, this -- I'm interested in the person who worked with you and not who received or prepared a peace agreement.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Fila, I said I can -- I could name one person with whom I worked during that time who received the peace agreement. And about that situation, the peace offer from the west. But I don't want to say whether that person worked with me or not. Because I worked with many people, I cannot really walk around and disclose people's identities to bring them into trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask the Court to go into private session so that we can elicit a response on whom he worked with, because Stanisic and Mijatovic were not there; that would be October 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand the witness to be saying that he wants to give the name of the person he was working with. I understood him to be saying he will not confirm the identity of the person he worked with after 1998. Now, are you understanding the position differently?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he said that he would mention the name of one of the persons and not of the other person. So it's something if we were to name one person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said a third thing. I said that I would name one operative, who on behalf of the service, received the document or information on the peace agreement for an early end of the war, and who took part in my expulsion from the country or my going abroad on a trip. That person may confirm that I was out on the ground, that I worked on certain tasks, and that that person received from me, on behalf of the service, the peace offer document. And this is the only circumstances that I can link that person with, because this is pertinent to this trial. As far as other operatives that I worked with or if I were to confirm that I continually worked with that person, at this, I do not want to confirm. And I ask the Bench to -- not to impose that obligation, because I may create trouble for those people back there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In relation to the person whose name you are willing to give, why must that be in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For security reasons, for the safety of that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. That's a good enough reason for us to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, my next question: Who gave you the tapes of the conversation between Sainovic and Lukic? What is the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody gave me those tapes. It was -- I was just allowed to listen to a part of the tape and I cannot name that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see, Your Honour, we still have this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: is going to illuminate this problem at least indirectly for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is very important for me to explain who gave you the whole tape, or at least a part of the tape; where, when, which place? Who, when, and where?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would jeopardise the life of that person, and it is understandable that I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a moment when you need to react, I believe, because otherwise I cannot continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, there's been a reference that needs to be redacted. I would ask you all, particularly the witness, who is the one concerned, to be cautious about reference to names. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I think that if the witness keeps this position in not revealing the names of the witnesses, for us, it would be also impossible to conduct the cross-examination of this witness, or we move -- that part of his statement would be redacted and not part of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, have you a number of questions of this nature?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it would help us to see the extent of the problem. So could you advance at the moment and we will reserve our decision on how to approach this until we see exactly the extent of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It may be that I can be of assistance. I'm not sure this is the kind of assistance you're asking for. In the witness's statement, at least 31 times he says his information came from unnamed SDB contacts. I can give you the paragraph numbers if that would be of assistance to you, and I think among the three of us, or four of us left, we probably will want answers on, firstly, all those paragraphs. I don't know if it would assist if you would have those paragraph numbers, but if it would, I can tell you what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's not necessary at the moment, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We may return to that. Just give me a moment while I look at my earlier notes. For me to say anything further about this, I think we again need to go into private session because there was -- it was discussed previously in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you have your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Paragraph 86 in the Serbian, since I'm using Serbian, you said the following: "From my western sources --" or "By my western sources, it was confirmed to me that there is at least one taped conversation in which Sainovic orders Lukic to kill Albanians." You never mentioned that elsewhere, did you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not done with your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I was waiting for the interpreters. In the discussion of the 4th and 5th of November, 2006, when you spoke to the OTP, you said the following: "My western sources and the SDB confirmed the existence of the taped conversations between Sainovic and Lukic, dating back to early 1999 in which Sainovic ordered Lukic" - listen carefully - "to attack the villages with Albanian population. I heard this conversation on a tape in the SDB." Yesterday, to Mr. Hannis's question, you said that the tape was gained by intercepting a conversation, and that you can hear on it that Sainovic exchanges views and issues instructions to Lukic concerning combat operations in that village, and later to remove all traces. You also said that Sainovic and Lukic were tapped and that western sources had such tapes containing Sainovic and Lukic's conversations. You also said that Radio B92 mentioned the existence of the tape - you didn't say whether it was radio or TV, actually - and that it can be seen that Sainovic issued instructions to Lukic so as how to remove the corpses from Racak, and before that concerning combat activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Time for a question, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you realise that these were different statements and that both were given under oath? And I can start all over again.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I insisted, concerning my previous statement that was amended, that changes be inserted. I may have used poor wording. I was probably too tired and speaking in English, and it would have been unfair on my part to say that Sainovic ordered Lukic to kill Kosovo Albanians. Certainly not, not the way that was formed. But the attack on a civilian village does boil down to having civilian casualties among the Kosovar Albanians. Therefore, I asked the Prosecutor, since this was not a very elegant formulation -- and it was pregnant with meaning. It seemed almost as Lukic and Sainovic were having a hand-gun killing Albanians. That's why I wanted it corrected, to the extent presented by the OTP, that there were instructions concerning the attack on the village, and in that village, apart from the terrorists, there was a large number of civilians, which boils down to the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another thing --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. At this point, in light of how it appears in the transcript, I think I need to read into the record the exact wording of the supplemental information on this paragraph, because it's slightly different than how it got interpreted from the B/C/S that Mr. Fila was speaking about. It reads: "My western sources have confirmed to me, et cetera, should read: 'My western and SDB sources confirmed a taped conversation between Sainovic and Lukic in early 1999 in which Sainovic directed Lukic to attack Kosovo Albanian villages. I heard a tape of this conversation at the SDB.'"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we're going to break again. Mr. Fila, I thought you were going to go through some paragraphs with a view to identifying who the sources were and then you would continue with your cross-examination. So we haven't really progressed the issue that's before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour, I said the very same thing Mr. Hannis quoted. I didn't put it any other way. Let us be clear on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, well, back to the point I'm making to you: I thought that you were going to go through some paragraphs and show me just how extensive this problem was going to be, but we haven't reached that stage yet. Hopefully we will sometime soon. We'll have to adjourn now until ten minutes to 1.00. Into closed session for the witness to leave, and we'll remain in closed session until we return.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We identified all paragraphs, but among the Defence, we have agreed that I will only address those pertaining to Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Ackerman will address the other paragraphs. And I'm prepared to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During your testimony, Mr. Tanic, you said that, through different SDB channels, you informed our people in Serbia that the RTS was to be bombed. My question is: Through what people did you inform the Serbian side; by what means? And please bear in mind that there is a letter by Goran Petrovic, who worked at the time of Rade Markovic, who says that within the SDB service there is no such information, and that is part of the record.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operative channels were identified before I left the country, and the person was identified in closed session. The information was provided via communications links, because I was abroad at the time, and I believe that is the answer to your question. As regards Goran Petrovic's position on it, I cannot comment. The information was forwarded and the other person was named in closed session, and it can be confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us understand something. As regards the aforementioned person, you said that you only gave him a plan when you went out in 1999. You know what I'm talking about. But you didn't say that you gave him information on the bombing of the RTS. That's what you stated here for the first time.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was an addition, so as to be cooperative and for the interests of justice. But we are talking about an operative, about a person who transmitted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell me when you gave it to him, and where.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, it was via communication means. I was abroad. I may be mistaken as to the exact date. It was taped. Since this is standard operating procedure, you can ask for a tape from our institutions, and then Mr. Petrovic will change his view.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As far as I know, Petrovic said no, and you have his letter in the file.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then summon the person identified in closed session. I cannot undertake the role of the Court here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm not asking you anything, Mr. Tanic, except to answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify that that person was not at the decision-making level. He was an operative and there was no time for any meetings. And we used the arranged means of communication that I had in place to communicate with the SDB, together with the codes and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is what I'm interested: Who established the means to be used? It was at a time when there was no Mijatovic or Stanisic. Who was it? Tell us the names of people you agreed on the codes, the means and how and when; if not, tell us you don't want to answer it and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've explained sufficiently. You can confirm that with the person who was mentioned during closed session, and you can ask him for more information since it didn't concern only the plan but generally. I just said that that person should not be held accountable for everything. He was not informed with everything. He was an operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, it wasn't done through him or with him but with someone higher up, as regards the means of communication, if I understand correctly; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you didn't understand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us try again. Who did you agree with on the plan of communication and means to be used as well as the codes to be used, if not that person?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that person could tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But that's not him.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't at that rank, at that level. He couldn't make such arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's what I asked you a moment ago. Was that plan put in writing as to the codes and the rest?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you know the nature of such work. What do you mean "in writing," that we signed on what we agreed? No. We used the codes. That was the only thing that was written down because you can't memorise everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, to conclude, you don't want to tell us the name of that person with whom you made that plan and who provided you with the codes; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, why is it you will not give that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'd like to apologise for interjecting before. I wasn't aware that you were still addressing the Defence. There are three reasons, the first being to protect the physical integrity; the second, these are intelligence things and at wartime it is very easy to go wrong on your assessment. And at this moment, this person may have been involved in the attempted murder of myself, maybe yes, maybe no. I start going into such theorising, I would put myself in a situation far too burdensome for any witness, and this was what the state of Serbia was supposed to do. And Goran Petrovic, as I learned now, denied that. When I met the minister of the interior, Mihajlovic, in Paris 2001, Goran Petrovic was there with him and I talked to Mihajlovic about Milosevic allowing intentionally for the bombing of the RTS. And Petrovic never denied that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now you're wandering from the subject. I'm asking you why you will not divulge the name. Now, the first reason was to protect the physical integrity. Is this someone who continues to work in the security service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You then say that -- if you start going into theorising, you would put yourself in a situation far too burdensome for any witness. What are you theorising about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I were to dwell on theories, who cooperated with whom during war, secret services cooperated quite a lot, ours with the foreign services, with us, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not being asked to theorised; you're only being asked for the facts. Do you appreciate that if anything is said in private session in this court that it's not open to anyone within the court to disclose that information, except to the extent that it is necessary for the purpose of investigating the case? Now, do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I also understand that the Defence knows that; and in that case, it's as if I published it openly. And apart from that, there is another reason. If I were to disclose such a thing, those persons will negate everything. Nobody is fool enough to admit to such things. I believe that the onus should be put more to the Prosecution and the Court. We are dealing with things that do exist. Everything was taped during the war, and if the state of Serbia does not want to provide those tapes and is offering lies, then there's no way for me to influence that and that is now the problem between the Tribunal and the state of Serbia. This is not my problem. If I were to name those persons with whom I worked, tomorrow those persons are going to send you statements that they never laid their eyes on me. And after that, you know what will happen to me. I'm in a witness protection programme together with my wife and child. Maybe that person had been threatened, maybe they've changed their opinion. We are dealing with turbulent times, and this is why I mentioned the parts of the tapes. I mentioned that I heard it and that never dwelled on how and what -- and parts of my communication were also taped. I know that my communication with the secret service while I was inside the country and outside the country were taped. These are important things to be taped. Everything exists in Serbia. If they don't want to provide that to The Hague Tribunal. For instance, now I heard for the first time in my life that Goran Petrovic is now negating things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it would be of any use, Your Honour, that person, Goran Petrovic, was head of the State Security Sector after the fall of Milosevic. He's now retired. He's alive and well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Milosevic spoke differently when he was with him. Of course he's alive and well and now he's denying everything. You know, Mr. Fila, what happens in Serbia, and the Court knows that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Your Honours allows me, I would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that, under the authority of SDB, you went to Hungary during the bombing. On two occasions you went abroad if I'm not very much mistaken?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, through Hungary to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. First you have to go through Hungary. In the trial of Milosevic -- in the Milosevic trial, during examination-in-chief, my learned colleague Nice asked you on whose decision you left the country during the bombing, and then you stated that pursuant to the decision of the joint staff of the defence of Belgrade, that is Milosevic trial transcript on the 15th of May, 2002, page 4969, lines 6 to 7, and 4970, lines 5 to 6.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During the war the command was integrated and persons from the area of Belgrade, where I lived, may leave the town only pursuant to a decision of the joint defence command of Belgrade. Everything was approved by Milosevic, and as far as has become known to the public, only two persons were involved in acceleration of end of war were involved. My person and Mr. Lilic, we achieved the same results. But the joint command -- joint staff is mentioned because this is a technical thing. I was a military conscript at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now we are coming to the part which I'd like to ask you about. You haven't mentioned this joint staff. Who is the person who ordered you to go abroad on these two occasions? Who paid for the trip? How much were you paid? And who did you report back to when you came back?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second person mentioned in private session may help you with this thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who told you to go abroad? Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It came from the very top of the service, and that top of the service must have consulted with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is the name, given name and family name, of the person who told you to go abroad in 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gentleman mentioned in private session may probably help you with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you don't want to say? You require that I ask that person mentioned in private session. Is this your position?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I was more than cooperative in such substantive issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who paid you and how much to go abroad?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SDB covered part of the expenses and the total expense reached some 10.000 German marks for the -- for both trips. They covered approximately half of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am asking you the name of the person who gave you this money.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the person mentioned in private session, the operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you report back to that staff or the SDB upon return?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Which?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person mentioned in private session may help you with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can we identify the dates of these visits that you're referring to, Mr. Fila? Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness asks us not to harp on him with regard to dates, and I'm trying to accommodate him. I'm not asking him whether it was a Monday or Tuesday. He said during the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you remember any dates? I don't want to harp on that too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, never mind the dates. If -- that's not important, but where were these visits to?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please explain what was it all about when you went abroad?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I can do that. Hungary, Italy, and United Kingdom, this is as far as I can say and I believe that this will more than suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Both times?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both times.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would it be useful for us to find out who you spoke to on these trips, if you wish to divulge?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly that can be -- that information can provide you with part of an answer by the ambassador, Italian ambassador to Belgrade, Ricardo Sosa, but he did not accompany me on those trips. He was in Belgrade -- well, during the second trip, he was abroad, but don't put your focus on Italy. No need to drag that country into this whole mess, and Mr. Milutinovic had a very well-established contacts with Italy, Italian ambassador, and he knows much about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On one associated matter, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, with regard to what you were asked by His Honour, you know that managers of the SDB were Rade Markovic and Radonjic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was one of them the person who sent you abroad?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You have to provide an answer, otherwise it will not enter the transcript.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you were kidnapped -- I'm not going to dwell on that. It must have been a terrifying experience. Do you know at whose orders or instructions from the top of SDB or was it SDB, or was it solely done by JSO?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mijatovic and Mihajlovic confirmed that it was on somebody else's, and they confirmed to me on 2001, when I had contacts with them. Mijatovic at the time was deputy head of the State Security Service and Mihajlovic was the minister of the police. They confirmed the identity of those persons and the participation of the JSO, and everything was taped anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm not going to force you to spell out their names, but you know who we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, of course I do know that. I know the name of the person who was in operational command of this whole action, and this is why I'm being so cautious.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, did they force you to sign anything that would involve the British secret service, something about your relations with the British secret service?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can open -- speak openly about that. Well, finally they had to come up with something because the Vuk Draskovic connection fell through. They wanted to get rid of us very quickly. I have to explain the circumstances, otherwise the Judges may think that I'm inventing things. So after this unsuccessful assassination attempt at Ibarska Maga Strela [phoen]. They came back, and I was completely disheveled. And it was evident that they tried to get of us very quickly, not to kill us but to have nothing to do with us anymore. And as I stated, I did not want to provide information on Stanisic, Mijatovic on camera -- no, no, wait. We are coming to that. They had to produce some results to their boss, you know. So since they could not elicit any admission as to the coup d'etat or any other thing, then finally they insisted that I take part of the responsibility on myself. And I said, Okay, it goes for me, my body, I can take part of the responsibility. But since I'd be involved in this for 25 years, I knew that they had to produce some results, provide some goods, otherwise the situation would have been worse. So I took some responsibility, but in a way which makes it certain that it was done under duress. I had a cynical smirk on my face. I mentioned people for whom it was known that they had nothing to do with it. You know, they had to have something on tape, on camera, but it is evident from my cynical smirk that I really did not mean what I was saying. I was providing loads of gibberish to them. They could not kill Vuk Draskovic so they had to make do with something.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: May I ask what all of that had to do with the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was whether they forced me to sign anything, with relation to the British security service. I did not sign anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. Yes. As I said, I -- they had to produce some goods --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where do I read in your answer that they made you sign something to do with the British secret service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, maybe it was completely precise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your description of gibberish may, to some extent, apply to some of the things you say in answer to some of these questions. Please concentrate on what the question is about. There's no answer to the question contained in that very long passage from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They did -- not to sign, but they wanted to some footage of me admitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I still don't know what you did. If you want to tell -- if you want me to make any finding about what was done to you on this occasion, you better tell me. Did you say something about the -- your connection with the British secret service, or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. But they knew that beforehand, because the SDB exchanged information with them through me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I just want the facts, Mr. Tanic. Are you ever going to get that into your head that we want to know the facts, what actually happened. So what was it you told them about your relations with the British Secret Service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then we should move into closed session, please. I can ask that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A moment ago you said, "Oh, yes, we can talk about that openly." Your very words. Now we're in private session for what reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because now you are asking me to dwell on details. I can give you a generalised answer in an open session. But now that you require me to provide details, I would to do so in private session or closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you wish this information, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I wanted to elicit information from him, whether he signed anything referring to himself and another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you state that about that other person or not?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not forced to sign anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, the question is not answered because the question ultimately was: Did you state that about that other person or not? Now, did you say something about another person on this tape or video?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it's better for us to move into private session and let -- let's have him say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I didn't want to ask you anything about Dusan Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be better if we moved into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we have to have reasons for going into closed session. This is a public trial. What is the reason for going into closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, don't ask me. I wanted to have it public; he didn't. I cannot go any further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You wanted to know whether I was asked anything about Dusan Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And about the service, because my research points to -- points in another direction. Did they asked you about the British Secret Service, about your membership, the person I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What person? Dusan Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just stop. This episode started off as questions about whether anything -- you were compelled to say anything about the British secret service. And we got a ramble answer that never mentioned the British secret service. Now we're trying to make progress beyond that stage, and the only point we've reached is something about Dusan Mihajlovic, which is totally vague to me. So nothing has come of the last five minutes of this court process. Let's rewind, Mr. Fila, start again, and if there is an issue that requires private session and there's a justification for it, we will go into it. But you take the lead because obviously I'm certainly going to cause confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us be confused together. The basic question: Why do we need to move into closed session for you to explain what they asked you and what you told them as regards the British secret service? That's what you need to tell us, and then a decision can be made.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was said was to confuse them, for me to be able to keep my head on my shoulders. These are yet some other operative techniques I employed to save my skin. I don't want to address that openly, but as regards Mihajlovic, I can address that openly. I just need to know what you want to do -- to know, Mihajlovic, the British secret service, the JSO. I'm confused. I apologise to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm not interested in the JSO. You answered as regards Dusan Mihajlovic. So the first question remains: What did you tell them about your work with the British security service?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lied to them in a way so as to render the material they gained worthless. That's why I wanted to explain this in detail in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is up to you, Your Honour. Should you decide we move -- we should move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is this information that's of any importance for the trial? No. Well, let's move on. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're all tired. I'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So do you want now to tell us what they -- what you told them? Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, there's no reason. If you wish this information, we shall go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You left the service after that, after the unfortunate event, and you left the country, if I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it can hardly be described as an unfortunate event. A month later, I left the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Fila's microphone was not on from the start.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm interested in this: Why didn't you return to the country when your Dusan Mihajlovic became minister, Goran Petrovic became the man number two, and Zoran Mijatovic the man number three? What prevented you from coming back?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thank you for that answer. I knew that the same people, who were most likely to kill me, helped these three come to power. And as it turned out I was right, because then Mr. Zoran Djindjic, the prime minister, was killed subsequently. You know very well, Mr. Fila - and it's not nice of you to hide that from the Bench - but you do know that the new government in Serbia was installed with the assistance of the special units.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Fila's microphone was not on from the start.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I had discussions with two members of that new government and later on abroad. And I was under the impression that they owe a lot to the JSO -- and let me complete the answer. Apart from that I saw Mihajlovic refuse to clear my name and to close my case. I asked from him, as minister of the police, to clear the situation as regards the torture and the kidnapping, to close the file, to clear my name. We needn't indict anyone. But let us settle the situation, because I knew they were behind some other murders. And I also asked that my debts be waived. I asked for the books and my wife's piano. I had asked for that in writing twice, and he did nothing. And now you are asking why I didn't go back. How can I go back when my party comrade, the minister of the police, cannot even do so much as to return my books and my wife's piano. And I spoke to him in Paris and he said: Ratko, just drop that and come back. And I realised that nothing would come of that and the remnants of Milosevic's regime are still there, behind the scenes, wielding power and force. And I was right and you can only judge that by Djindjic's murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At that meeting in Paris, were you at that time employed by the British secret service as well?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Escorted by the British secret service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But there were French operatives there, secured by Mijatovic or someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't on good terms with Mijatovic. What were the reasons for you to start collaborating with the SDB? Did you do that for money, for ideology?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of my ideas and my political beliefs. At that time I was gaging myself in politics; therefore, ideology reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, just a moment. There's an answer there that's quite inconsistent with what was said. The question was: At that meeting at Paris, were you at that time employed -- sorry, escorted by the British secret service. Now, what was your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I was not, but as I learned subsequently, there were French operatives, the French Secret Service, and I learned that from Mijatovic's book. They were there, around, at least that's what he said, but that may not be true. I wasn't escorted by anyone. I just went there to see my former head of party and the then-minister of police, to see if he could help me with my property --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that on several occasions you met with Mijatovic. Is it correct that in 1995, in restaurant Vusce [Realtime transcript read in error "Vustrin"], he paid you 2.000 Deutschemarks.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true, and that was to cover expenses. The name of the restaurant is Vusce, V-u-s-c-e. The interpretation is incorrect. It was in 1995, and I've known him and them since the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you receive money on several occasions, and from whom, on the part of the SDB?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. On several occasions, to cover expenses, apart from the time of war when another person paid the money out to me. Before that, Mijatovic gave money to me on two or three occasions, and this was to cover expenses. It was no fee of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
